pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Naming Everyday Materials

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 'Everyday materials'):** Pupils should be taught to "identify and name a variety of everyday materials, including wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, and rock." Non-statutory guidance adds further materials to meet through exploration — "brick, paper, fabrics and elastic" — and expects pupils to "explore, name, discuss and raise and answer questions about everyday materials so that they become familiar with the names of materials."

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-1, partial anchor):** NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to naming materials; naming is treated as embedded vocabulary within DCI PS1.A — "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]" — which anchors 2-PS1-1 ("[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]").

- **Operational details:** Build a shared spoken vocabulary of the six statutory materials plus common extras (paper, fabric, brick, elastic) through repeated exposure to real samples children handle and name. Anchor each material word to a set of varied exemplars — wood as a block, a spoon, a door and a pencil — so the name attaches to the substance, not to one object. Run naming hunts around the room ('find me three things made of metal') and record findings in a simple frequency table. Explicitly revisit that some objects are made of more than one material, so naming does not collapse back into 'one object, one word'.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can name at least six everyday materials (wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, rock), identify the material of ten or more real objects, and point to one object made from more than one material — evidence the material names are secure and attached to substances.
bestPractices: Anchor each material name to several varied objects (wood = block, spoon, door) so the word names the substance, not a single item — directly countering the object/material conflation.
Give children real samples to handle, look at and talk about; naming is learned by repeated multisensory exposure at KS1, not from a word list.
Run active naming hunts ('find three metal things') and log results in a frequency table to consolidate the vocabulary and reveal which materials are common.
Deliberately include the tricky cases — water and rock — as materials, since children resist calling a liquid or a natural solid a 'material'.
Contrast near-neighbours (glass vs clear plastic, metal vs shiny plastic) so the name is tied to the true material, not just to appearance.
Name the extra everyday materials from the non-statutory list (paper, fabric, brick, elastic) so vocabulary breadth matches the curriculum's intent.
keyRepresentations: Sets of real samples grouped by material (a 'wood tray', a 'metal tray')
A picture-and-audio material word bank: wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, rock (+ paper, fabric, brick, elastic)
A material naming hunt with a frequency-table tally sheet
Multiple varied objects sharing one material, displayed together to fix the name to the substance
Near-neighbour pairs (glass vs clear plastic; metal vs shiny grey plastic) for discrimination
commonMisconceptions: 'Material' means only cloth/fabric, so children fail to name glass, metal, water or rock as materials.
Water is not a material because it is a liquid, not a solid 'thing'.
Rock and stone are different materials, when 'stone' is just a word for smaller pieces of rock.
A material name is tied to one object (wood = 'a pencil') rather than to the substance shared by many objects.
All plastic is hard and all metal is silver, so children misname materials by a single expected appearance.

learn.summary: For children aged 5–6 learning to name everyday materials (wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, rock, plus paper, fabric, brick, elastic). The teaching objective is to attach each material word to the substance shared by many different objects — not to a single item — through handling and naming real exemplars, active naming hunts, and deliberate work on the tricky cases (water and rock) and look-alike pairs (glass vs clear plastic; metal vs shiny grey plastic). Build spoken vocabulary; no reading required.

activities.title: Name the material: one word, many objects
feedback: When several objects are grouped and each named 'wood', confirm: 'All of these are made of wood — wood is the stuff, not just one object.'
If the child names only one object per word, prompt: 'What else here is made of the same material?'
For the pencil or similar, point out it is made of more than one material so naming does not collapse into one-object-one-word.
activities.rationale: Naming is a vocabulary-to-referent mapping; anchoring each word to several varied exemplars directly counters the object/material conflation, and deliberately naming water and rock targets their documented exclusion. In an optional on-screen version, tapping an object can speak its material name while every same-material object gently glows — making the name-to-substance link visible — but the same insight is available with real samples sorted into material trays.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y1 statutory requirement: pupils taught to 'identify and name a variety of everyday materials, including wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, and rock'; non-statutory extras brick, paper, fabrics, elastic.
Documented KS1 misconceptions: 'material' meaning only fabric; water/rock resisted as materials; rock vs stone confusion; all plastic hard / all metal silver.
learnerActions: Handle and name a set of real objects, saying what each one is MADE of (e.g. a wooden door, a wooden spoon, a wooden ruler, wooden toy blocks).
Group objects that share a material together so the child sees the same word — 'wood' — belongs to several different objects.
Deliberately include a cup/puddle of water and a garden stone, naming water and rock aloud as materials.
Point to and name one object that is made of more than one material (e.g. a pencil with an eraser on top: wood, pencil 'lead' (graphite), paint, a metal band and a rubber eraser).
activities.intendedInsight: A material name refers to the substance something is made of, and one material word belongs to many different objects, whatever the object's shape or use.

activities.title: Material hunt with a tally
feedback: If a multi-material object is tallied once, prompt: 'Is this made of just one material? Where else could it go?'
Celebrate correct finds by restating the material word; redirect misnamed finds by asking what the object is made of.
After tallying, ask what the table shows: 'Which material did we find most of?'
activities.rationale: Active hunting and tallying is intended to consolidate vocabulary through doing and to show which materials were found most often in the space searched. An optional drag-to-sort on-screen version (objects dropped into labelled bins with a live-updating tally, multi-material objects placed in two bins) turns the same activity into a self-checking game, but the paper tally works equally well. No cited source claim directly evidences this method as superior, so it is offered as a research-informed proposal.
learnerActions: Go on a naming hunt around the room: find as many things made of metal as you can in a set time, then do the same for wood, and so on. Give every material the same amount of time and don't set a fixed number.
Record each find in a simple frequency table, tallying how many objects of each material are found.
For an object made of more than one material, record it under each of its materials.
Look at the finished tally and say which materials you found most often in the place you searched.
activities.intendedInsight: Materials are all around us, and an open-ended hunt can show which materials turn up most often in a particular place; active, repeated naming in use is intended to make the vocabulary more secure than reciting a list alone.

activities.title: Water, rock and the look-alike test
feedback: If the child leaves out the water, say: 'A material is what something is made of in any state — the sea, a puddle and ice are all the material water.'
If the child treats 'rock' as only one object, show rock across several objects: same material, different things.

If a clear plastic cup is called 'glass', or a shiny plastic object 'metal', invite the fair check: 'Tap it and feel it — does it behave like glass/metal or like plastic?' and note the check is a clue, not a final answer.

If the child thinks all metal is silver or all plastic is hard, show a dull or coloured metal object and a soft plastic one: 'This is still metal even though it is not shiny; this is still plastic even though it is soft.'
activities.rationale: Children commonly exclude water and rock and name look-alikes by appearance (clear = glass, shiny = metal), and also assume metal must be silver and plastic must be hard. Directly seeding these cases in both directions and introducing a simple behaviour-based clue targets the documented misconceptions. Asking 'how do you know?' after each look-alike decision can show whether the child understands where one material ends and another begins, or has just memorised answers.
sourceClaims: Documented KS1 misconceptions: 'material' meaning only fabric; water/rock resisted as materials; rock vs stone confusion; all plastic hard / all metal silver.
learnerActions: Confirm that water is a material: name the sea, a puddle and ice as all being the material water.
Confirm that rock is a material shared by many objects (a stone wall, a stone statue, a stone kerb, gravel), and that rock and stone are the same material.
Compare near-neighbour pairs — a glass jar and a clear plastic cup, and a metal object and a shiny grey plastic one — and decide which is which.

Name a metal object that is not shiny or not silver-coloured (e.g. a rusty iron nail, or a copper-coloured coin, which may be shiny but is not silver), and point out that not all plastic is hard — so a material cannot be judged by one expected look.

Use a quick check beyond looking: tap it, feel its weight and how cold it feels, and gently see if it bends (never try to bend glass) — and name the material by how it behaves, remembering this check is a helpful clue rather than a certain test.
activities.intendedInsight: A material is what something is made of in any state and wherever it comes from, so liquids and natural solids count; and material is judged by how it behaves and feels, not by appearance alone (clear is not always glass; shiny is not always metal; metal need not be shiny; plastic need not be hard).

constraints: All tasks should use spoken words, pictures and real objects — no reading required at age 5–6.

Picture multiple-choice, object→material matching and categorisation tasks can check whether the names are recognised, but recognition tasks do not by themselves elicit the child producing the material name aloud; use them as a check-up alongside handling and hunting rather than as the main teaching.

On-screen tap-to-reveal, glow highlighting, drag-to-sort bins and live tallies are optional ways to make the name-to-substance mechanism concrete; they are examples, not required, and real samples sorted into trays achieve the same aim.
A behaviour check (tap, feel weight/temperature, test bending) is a quick classroom clue to move past appearance; it is not a definitive material identification method.
Keep the broad meaning of 'material' explicit throughout, so children do not reserve the word for cloth/fabric.
Always include at least one multi-material object so naming does not collapse into one-object-one-word.

Include both look-alike pairs (glass vs clear plastic AND metal vs shiny grey plastic), and at least one non-shiny metal and one soft plastic, so naming is tied to the true material, not to a single expected appearance.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled open dialogue and 3D/spatial formats as adding 'no naming power' for this topic. That is a scoped fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; this rewrite does not reproduce it as a universal claim. Free conversation is a weaker fit for teaching a fixed vocabulary to pre-readers, and spatial manipulation is not central to attaching a word to a substance, but neither is categorically incapable of supporting learning.
The original 'ideal' tap-to-reveal recommendation is preserved as an optional interaction example rather than asserted as necessary; a static display of grouped exemplars can teach the same insight.
Two of the three cited sources (NGSS DCI PS1.A, STEM Learning/Oak misconceptions) are marked verified:false in the row; treat the misconception and NGSS claims as unverified pending review.
Activity 2's sourceClaims were set to [] because no exact sources[].claim directly supports the hunt-and-tally method; the DfE claim supports naming the materials but not this teaching method.

The DfE claim is kept on Activity 1 because it directly lists the materials the child handles and names there; the exemplar-anchoring principle itself rests on the misconception claim, not the DfE claim.
brick and elastic appear in the summary vocabulary but are not exemplified in a specific activity action; add exemplars if full breadth is required when scoring.

The assessment field notes paper and fabric among the 'clear cases' a child should name for full credit; confirm this matches the age-appropriate statutory core (wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, rock) plus non-statutory extras when scoring.

probeDeeper: Ice, water and steam — are they all the same material, or different materials? (state doesn't change the material)
This clear cup — is it glass or plastic? How could we find out for sure rather than just looking?
Is air a material? What makes you say so?
Name something made of metal that is NOT shiny or silver.
assess.correctAnswer: Names wood, plastic, glass, metal, paper and fabric for the clear cases; recognises that WATER and ROCK are also materials — a material is what something is made of, whatever its state or where it comes from.

errorPatterns.pattern: Water isn't a material — 'materials' must be solid (and usually man-made), so a liquid doesn't count.
errorPatterns.nextMove: State the rule: a material is what something is made of, in any state — the sea, a puddle and ice are all the material water; connect to States of Matter vocabulary.
errorPatterns.distractor: Water isn't a material, it's just a liquid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Leaves the cup of water out when naming materials; says 'that's just a liquid, not a material'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rock/stone isn't a material (or rock and stone are two different things) — natural, un-manufactured stuff is excluded.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show rock as the material of many objects (a stone wall, a statue, a kerb, gravel) — same material, different objects — and note rock and stone are the same material.
errorPatterns.distractor: A rock isn't a material — it's just a rock.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Excludes the pebble; treats 'rock' as a kind of object rather than a material.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Material' means only fabric/cloth — so of the tray, only the sock is a 'material'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the object/material distinction with the broad meaning of 'material' (whatever a thing is made of), naming the material of each item on the tray.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked which are materials, points only to the woolly sock.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names material by appearance alone — calls a clear plastic cup 'glass', or any shiny thing 'metal'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce a quick fair check (tap it, feel its weight/temperature, does it bend) so material is judged by behaviour, not just looks.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Mislabels a clear plastic item as glass, or shiny plastic as metal.

responseLevels.gap: Names only a few solid, manufactured materials; denies water and rock are materials; may reserve 'material' for cloth.
responseLevels.full: Names materials reliably INCLUDING water and rock, distinguishes look-alikes by more than appearance, and recognises the same material can appear across different objects and states.
responseLevels.partial: Names the six-plus everyday materials for clear-cut solid objects, but hesitates over or excludes water/rock, or labels look-alikes by appearance (clear = glass).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out about eight things: a wooden block, a plastic toy, a glass jar, a metal key, a cup of water, a pebble, a sheet of paper, a woolly sock. Say: 'Tell me what each one is MADE of.' Then hold up the water and the pebble: 'Is water a material? Is a rock a material? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The water and rock cases are the pivot: a child who has merely memorised a list of solid, manufactured 'materials' excludes them, while a child who understands material = what a thing is made of includes them. The tier-2 'how do you know?' exposes whether the boundary is rule-based or memorised.
